{{Short description|Theorem in abstract algebra}}
In [[abstract algebra]], the '''Eakin–Nagata theorem''' states: given [[commutative ring]]s <math>A \subset B</math> such that <math>B</math> is [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] as a [[module (mathematics)|module]] over <math>A</math>, if <math>B</math> is a [[Noetherian ring]], then <math>A</math> is a Noetherian ring.<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|loc=Theorem 3.7. (i)}}</ref> (Note the [[converse (logic)|converse]] is also true and is easier.)

The theorem is similar to the [[Artin–Tate lemma]], which says that the same statement holds with "Noetherian" replaced by "[[finitely generated algebra]]" (assuming the base [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] is a Noetherian ring).

The theorem was first [[mathematical proof|proved]] in Paul M. Eakin's thesis {{harv|Eakin|1968}} and later independently by {{harvs|first=Masayoshi|last=Nagata|authorlink=Masayoshi Nagata|year=1968|txt}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|loc=A remark after Theorem 3.7.}}</ref> The theorem can also be deduced from the [[Noetherian_ring#Implication_on_injective_modules|characterization of a Noetherian ring in terms of injective modules]], as done for example by [[David Eisenbud]] in {{harv|Eisenbud|1970}}; this approach is useful for a generalization to [[non-commutative ring]]s.<!-- the article needs to mention some results in the non-commutative case -->

== Proof ==
The following more general result is due to [[Edward W. Formanek]] and is proved by an argument rooted to the original proofs by Eakin and Nagata. According to {{harv|Matsumura|1989}}, this formulation is likely the most transparent one.

{{math_theorem|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|loc=Theorem 3.6.}}</ref> Let <math>A</math> be a commutative ring and <math>M</math> a [[faithful module|faithful]] finitely generated module over it. If the [[ascending chain condition]] holds on the [[submodule]]s of the form <math>IM</math> for [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]] <math>I \subset A</math>, then <math>A</math> is a Noetherian ring.}}

''Proof'': It is enough to show that <math>M</math> is a [[Noetherian module]] since, in general, a ring admitting a faithful Noetherian module over it is a Noetherian ring.<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|loc=Theorem 3.5.}}</ref> Suppose otherwise. By assumption, the set of all <math>IM</math>, where <math>I</math> is an ideal of <math>A</math> such that <math>M/IM</math> is not Noetherian has a maximal element, <math>I_0 M</math>. Replacing <math>M</math> and <math>A</math> by <math>M/I_0 M</math> and <math>A/\operatorname{Ann}(M/I_0 M)</math>, we can assume
*for each nonzero ideal <math>I \subset A</math>, the module <math>M/IM</math> is Noetherian.
Next, consider the set <math>S</math> of submodules <math>N \subset M</math> such that <math>M/N</math> is faithful. Choose a set of generators <math>\{ x_1, \dots, x_n \}</math> of <math>M</math> and then note that <math>M/N</math> is faithful [[if and only if]] for each <math>a \in A</math>, the inclusion <math>\{ a x_1, \dots, a x_n \} \subset N</math> implies <math>a = 0</math>. Thus, it is clear that [[Zorn's lemma]] applies to the set <math>S</math>, and so the set has a maximal element, <math>N_0</math>. Now, if <math>M/N_0</math> is Noetherian, then it is a faithful Noetherian module over ''A'' and, consequently, ''A'' is a Noetherian ring, a contradiction. Hence, <math>M/N_0</math> is not Noetherian and replacing <math>M</math> by <math>M/N_0</math>, we can also assume
*each nonzero submodule <math>N \subset M</math> is such that <math>M/N</math> is not faithful.
Let a submodule <math>0 \ne N \subset M</math> be given. Since <math>M/N</math> is not faithful, there is a nonzero element <math>a \in A</math> such that <math>aM \subset N</math>. By assumption, <math>M/aM</math> is Noetherian and so <math>N/aM</math> is finitely generated. Since <math>aM</math> is also finitely generated, it follows that <math>N</math> is finitely generated; i.e., <math>M</math> is Noetherian, a contradiction. <math>\square</math>
